newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corporate debt spreads flat, Marvel recoups.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corporate debt spreads flat, Marvel recoups.

text.p: U.S. corporate bond spreads were flat in thin trade as dealers focused on another $1.0 billion day of supply, while Marvel Entertainment Group's debt had high-yield players caught in a web of rumors, dealers said.

Street talk of prospective suitors of Marvel, holder of Marvel comic book characters Spiderman and the X-Men, helped drive its debt prices up three points in light trade, according to several traders. The same traders conceded talk was cheap and the debt had already been on a tear from lows seen on Wednesday, however.
Disney Inc and Time Warner Inc were two names bandied about in the Street on Friday, according to traders. Disney talk suggested a deal price of $6 per share, a trader said.
Marvel Holdings Inc's "old" bonds were quoted at 24-1/2 bid, 25-1/2 offer while the Marvel (Parent) Holdings Inc's "new" bonds were quoted at 22-1/2 near the close.

Those levels are still cheap relative to the stock, which rose 3/8 point to 3-1/4 on Friday, said Phelps Hoyt, vice president of KDP Investment Advisors Inc's fixed-income research group. At the current share price, Hoyt calculated relative values of 26 on the "olds" and 30 on the "news."

Marvel shares and debt sank on Tuesday after investor Ronald Perelman's Andrews Group Inc offered to buy 80.1 percent of new Marvel common stock for $350 million, far below market cost. The acquisition would be paid for in cash and/or Toy Biz TNZ.N stock, Andrews said.
The deal would dilute current stock which backs the outstanding Marvel debt.

The bonds were also up strong on Thursday, traders said, following news minority shareholders had filed lawsuits seeking to block Marvel from selling the new shares to Perelman, who is already a controlling shareholder.
Other high-yield trade was quiet by comparison with prices little changed to weaker, traders said.

Turning to investment grade trade, dealers reported equally quiet secondary activity with all attention geared toward another $1.0 billion day of new issues. The issuance had yet to significantly pressure spreads, but some market participants contended syndicates were still saddled with bonds from deals as far back as October.
One player suggested year-end selling caused some back-up, but that it did not portend any prolonged negative direction.
"A couple of bigger dealers are bidding stuff back a little, but particularly in high-grade land people think the market is going to do well and take that as an opportunity," one buy-sider said.
New issues featured a $500 million Yankee Baa1/single-A rated two-part deal from Southern Investments U.K. Plc via lead manager Lehman Brothers.

In the deal, a $168 million tranche of five-year notes were priced as 6-3/8s to yield 48 basis points over the Treasury curve and another $332 million 10-year notes were priced as 6.80s to yield 68 basis points over.
Elsewhere, CNA Financial Corp issued $250 million A3/A-minus rated 10-year notes as 6-3/4s to yield 63 basis points over Treasuries. Merrill Lynch & Co Inc is lead manager.
Finally, Coca-Cola Enterprises tapped the market with $250 million A3/A-minus rated 30-year debentures as 6.95s to yield 63 basis points over Treasuries. UBS Securities Inc managed the deal.
In U.S. Treasuries, the long bond closed off 17/32 to yield 6.36 percent after a spate of profit-taking, analysts said.
